chapter_text:
CHAPTER 5 — ATOMIC STRUCTURE

Introduction

In Chapter 3 we treated the atom as the smallest indivisible particle of an element. By the end of the 19th and early 20th centuries, experiments revealed that the atom itself has a rich internal structure: a tiny dense nucleus made of protons and neutrons, with electrons moving around it. This chapter traces that discovery — from Dalton's indivisible atom, through the cathode-ray and gold-foil experiments, to the modern Bohr picture — and develops the rules for electron arrangement (the '2n² rule' and valency).

5.1 DALTON'S ATOMIC THEORY AND ITS LIMITATIONS

Dalton (1803) proposed that:
 - All matter is made of indivisible particles called atoms.
 - Atoms of the same element are identical (same mass and properties).
 - Atoms of different elements differ.
 - Atoms combine in small whole-number ratios to form compounds.
 - In a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed.

Dalton's theory beautifully explained the laws of conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions. But subsequent experiments revealed limitations: atoms are NOT indivisible — they have internal structure (electrons, protons, neutrons); atoms of the same element can differ in mass (isotopes); atoms of different elements can have the same mass (isobars).

5.2 DISCOVERY OF SUBATOMIC PARTICLES

(a) Electron — J. J. Thomson, 1897.
Using a CATHODE RAY TUBE — a glass tube containing gas at very low pressure with electrodes at the ends — Thomson applied a high voltage and observed rays travelling from the cathode (negative electrode) to the anode (positive electrode). He showed these CATHODE RAYS were deflected by electric and magnetic fields, proving they were negatively charged particles. He named them ELECTRONS. The electron's mass-to-charge ratio was the same regardless of the gas or electrode material — so electrons are a UNIVERSAL constituent of all atoms.
  Electron properties: mass ≈ 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; charge = −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; relative charge −1; symbol e.

(b) Proton — Eugen Goldstein, 1886 (anode rays), later refined by Rutherford 1917.
Using a perforated cathode (one with holes) in a low-pressure discharge tube, Goldstein observed rays travelling from anode to cathode — the ANODE RAYS (or canal rays). These were positively charged particles, and their mass-to-charge ratio depended on the gas in the tube. With hydrogen, the particle had the smallest mass — this particle is the PROTON.
  Proton properties: mass ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (about 1836 times the electron's); charge = +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; relative charge +1; symbol p.

(c) Neutron — James Chadwick, 1932.
Following earlier hints from beryllium-bombardment experiments, Chadwick identified an electrically NEUTRAL particle with mass nearly equal to that of the proton. He named it the NEUTRON.
  Neutron properties: mass ≈ 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; charge = 0; symbol n.

A summary table:
  Particle  Symbol  Mass (kg)              Relative charge
  Electron  e       9.11 × 10⁻³¹           −1
  Proton    p       1.673 × 10⁻²⁷          +1
  Neutron   n       1.675 × 10⁻²⁷           0

5.3 THOMSON'S MODEL — THE 'PLUM PUDDING'

Given that atoms are electrically neutral and contain electrons, J. J. Thomson proposed (1903) that an atom is a uniformly POSITIVELY-CHARGED SPHERE with electrons embedded throughout it — like plums in a pudding (or seeds in a watermelon).
Drawback: Thomson's model could not explain the results of the α-ray scattering experiment that came a few years later.

5.4 RUTHERFORD'S NUCLEAR MODEL

In 1909, Geiger and Marsden (under Rutherford's guidance) fired a stream of α-particles (helium nuclei, He²⁺) at a very thin sheet of gold foil.

Observations:
 (1) Most α-particles passed STRAIGHT THROUGH the foil with no deflection.
 (2) A few were deflected through small angles.
 (3) A very few (about 1 in 8000) bounced BACK at large angles — as if they had hit something very dense.

Thomson's plum-pudding model could not explain (3) — a uniform 'pudding' would not deflect anything strongly. Rutherford (1911) proposed a new model:
 - An atom has a tiny, dense, POSITIVELY-CHARGED NUCLEUS at the centre.
 - The nucleus contains essentially all the atom's MASS and all its positive charge.
 - The electrons revolve around the nucleus in mostly EMPTY SPACE.
 - The atom's diameter is ~10⁻¹⁰ m, but the nucleus is only ~10⁻¹⁵ m across — so the atom is mostly empty.

Drawbacks of Rutherford's model:
 (i) According to Maxwell's electromagnetic theory, a charged particle in circular motion (the orbiting electron) continuously radiates energy and would spiral into the nucleus. But atoms are stable — they don't collapse.
 (ii) The model says nothing about HOW electrons are distributed around the nucleus.
 (iii) It cannot explain the discrete spectral lines emitted by excited atoms.

5.5 BOHR'S MODEL (1913)

Niels Bohr modified Rutherford's model with two postulates:

Postulate 1: Electrons revolve in DEFINITE CIRCULAR ORBITS (also called energy levels or shells) around the nucleus. While in these orbits, the electron does NOT radiate energy. Shells are labelled K, L, M, N, ... (or by integer n = 1, 2, 3, 4, ...). The K shell (n = 1) has the lowest energy.

Postulate 2: An electron can JUMP between shells — but only by absorbing or emitting a single photon whose energy equals the difference between the two shells. Going FROM low TO high energy requires absorbing a photon: E_photon = hν = E_f − E_i. Going from high to low emits a photon of the same energy.

This explains atomic stability (electrons in allowed orbits don't radiate) and the discrete spectral lines (only certain photon energies are possible).

5.6 ATOMIC NUMBER AND MASS NUMBER

Already introduced in Chapter 3 and revisited here:
 - ATOMIC NUMBER Z = number of protons in the nucleus = number of electrons in a neutral atom.
 - MASS NUMBER A = number of protons + number of neutrons (nucleons).
 - Number of neutrons N = A − Z.
 - Atomic notation: ᴬZX. For example ¹²C means carbon with A = 12, Z = 6 (so 6 protons, 6 electrons, 6 neutrons).

5.7 DISTRIBUTION OF ELECTRONS IN SHELLS (BOHR-BURY RULE)

Electrons are filled into shells starting from the lowest-energy shell (K, n = 1) and proceeding outward. The maximum number of electrons that the n-th shell can hold is given by:

   maximum = 2n²

  Shell  n  Maximum capacity
   K     1  2 × 1² = 2
   L     2  2 × 2² = 8
   M     3  2 × 3² = 18
   N     4  2 × 4² = 32

A further refinement (the Bohr–Bury rule) states that the OUTERMOST shell can hold at most 8 electrons, and the SECOND-OUTERMOST at most 18 (or 32 for very heavy atoms). Once the outer shell has 8 electrons (or 2 for K), a new shell begins.

Electronic configuration: the list of electron counts in each shell, written 2, 8, 8, ... for shells K, L, M, ... For example:
 - Hydrogen (Z = 1): 1
 - Helium (Z = 2): 2 (K shell full)
 - Carbon (Z = 6): 2, 4
 - Oxygen (Z = 8): 2, 6
 - Sodium (Z = 11): 2, 8, 1
 - Calcium (Z = 20): 2, 8, 8, 2

5.8 VALENCE ELECTRONS AND VALENCY

The electrons in the OUTERMOST shell are called VALENCE ELECTRONS. They determine the chemical behaviour of the atom — chemistry is the science of how outer electrons rearrange when atoms react.

Valency (the combining capacity) is determined as follows:
 - If the number of valence electrons is 4 OR FEWER, the valency equals the number of valence electrons.
   Example: Sodium (1 valence electron) → valency 1; Aluminium (3 valence electrons) → valency 3.
 - If the number of valence electrons is MORE THAN 4, the valency = 8 − (valence electrons).
   Example: Oxygen (6 valence electrons) → valency 8 − 6 = 2; Chlorine (7) → valency 8 − 7 = 1.
 - Noble gases (helium: 2 valence electrons; neon, argon: 8) have ZERO valency because their outer shells are FULL — they have no tendency to react.

SUMMARY

- Dalton's atom was indivisible; experiments later showed atoms contain electrons (Thomson), protons (Goldstein/Rutherford) and neutrons (Chadwick).
- Thomson's plum-pudding model — uniform positive sphere with electrons embedded — was disproved by Rutherford's α-scattering experiment.
- Rutherford's nuclear model: tiny dense positive nucleus + electrons in surrounding empty space. Its drawback: instability and silence about electron distribution.
- Bohr's two postulates: electrons live in discrete orbits (no radiation while in orbit); they jump between orbits by absorbing or emitting a photon.
- Atomic number Z = protons = electrons (neutral atom); mass number A = protons + neutrons.
- Electrons fill shells outward; max per shell = 2n²; outermost shell ≤ 8.
- Valency: if valence electrons ≤ 4, valency = count; if > 4, valency = 8 − count.

chapter_summary.title: Atomic Structure — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 5. It traces the development of atomic models from Dalton's indivisible atom through Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr, introduces the three subatomic particles (electron, proton, neutron) and their discoveries, and gives the rules for electronic configuration (2n²) and valency.

sections.heading: Dalton's theory and its limitations
bullets: According to Dalton's atomic theory, the atom is the smallest indivisible constituent of matter. It explained conservation of mass, constant composition and multiple proportions.
Later experiments showed atoms have internal structure (electrons, protons, neutrons), so Dalton's 'indivisible' postulate had to be revised.
Isotopes (atoms of the same element with different masses) violate Dalton's 'atoms of the same element are identical' postulate.
Isobars (different elements with same mass number) violate the idea that mass is unique to each element.

sections.heading: Discovery of the electron, proton and neutron
bullets: J. J. Thomson (1897) discovered the electron using a CATHODE RAY TUBE: cathode rays travel from cathode to anode and are deflected by electric/magnetic fields, proving they are negatively charged particles.
Eugen Goldstein (1886) used a perforated cathode in a discharge tube to find anode rays — establishing the existence of the positively charged PROTON in atoms.
James Chadwick (1932) discovered the NEUTRON — an electrically neutral particle in the nucleus, mass nearly equal to the proton's.
Electron: mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, relative charge −1. Proton: mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, relative charge +1. Neutron: mass 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 0.

sections.heading: Thomson's plum-pudding model and its failure
bullets: According to Thomson's plum-pudding model, an atom is a large sphere of uniform positive charge with a number of small negatively charged electrons scattered throughout — like plums in a pudding.
The α-ray scattering experiment performed by Geiger and Marsden caused the failure of Thomson's model.
A uniform 'pudding' cannot explain why some α-particles bounce back at large angles.

sections.heading: Rutherford's nuclear model
bullets: α-particles fired at a thin gold foil mostly passed through; some were deflected by small angles; very few rebounded backward — implying a tiny, dense, positively charged region inside the atom.
Rutherford (1911): the atom has a dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre. Electrons revolve around it in mostly empty space.
All the positive charge and most of the mass are contained in the nucleus.

Drawbacks: a circling electron should continuously radiate (Maxwell's theory) and spiral into the nucleus — but atoms are stable. The model also doesn't specify HOW the electrons are arranged or explain atomic spectra.

sections.heading: Bohr's model
bullets: Postulate 1: Electrons move in DEFINITE circular orbits (energy levels / shells) labelled K, L, M, N, ... or n = 1, 2, 3, 4, .... While in these orbits, the electron does not radiate energy. The K shell (n = 1) is the lowest in energy.

Postulate 2: The electron can change shells by absorbing or releasing energy. Moving from lower to higher level requires absorbing a photon of energy hν = E_f − E_i; moving the other way emits a photon of the same energy.
Bohr's model explains both atomic stability and the discrete spectral lines emitted by excited atoms.

sections.heading: Atomic number, mass number, electronic configuration and valency
bullets: Atomic number Z = number of protons = number of electrons (in a neutral atom).
Mass number A = number of nucleons = protons + neutrons.
An atom X with atomic number Z and mass number A is denoted as ᴬZX.

The maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by 2n², where n is the shell number: K (n=1) → 2, L (n=2) → 8, M (n=3) → 18, N (n=4) → 32. The outermost shell additionally cannot hold more than 8 electrons.

Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell. If their number is ≤ 4, valency = that number. If > 4, valency = 8 − (number of valence electrons). Noble gases have valency 0 (full outer shell).

key_takeaways: Dalton's indivisible atom was modified after the discovery of subatomic particles — electron (Thomson, 1897), proton (Goldstein, 1886), neutron (Chadwick, 1932).
Thomson's plum-pudding model failed because α-particle scattering showed atoms are mostly empty with a dense nucleus.
Rutherford's nuclear model fixed the geometry but couldn't explain atomic stability; Bohr's quantised orbits supplied that fix.
Atomic number Z = protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons; isotopes share Z, isobars share A.
Electrons fill K, L, M, N shells outward, with maximum 2n² per shell and ≤ 8 in the outermost.
Valency: if valence electrons ≤ 4, valency = count; if > 4, valency = 8 − count. Noble gases (full outer shell) have valency 0.

glossary.definition: The smallest particle of an element that retains its chemical properties; once thought to be indivisible, now known to have internal structure.
A negatively-charged subatomic particle of very small mass (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg). Discovered by J. J. Thomson in 1897 using the cathode-ray tube. Relative charge −1.
A positively-charged subatomic particle with mass ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (about 1836 times the electron's). Resides in the nucleus. Relative charge +1.
An electrically neutral subatomic particle with mass nearly equal to the proton's; resides in the nucleus. Discovered by Chadwick in 1932.
A stream of electrons produced when a high voltage is passed across electrodes in a low-pressure gas tube; deflected by electric/magnetic fields.
A stream of positively-charged particles produced in a discharge tube with a perforated cathode; led to the discovery of the proton.
An early atomic model that pictured the atom as a large sphere of uniform positive charge with electrons embedded throughout — disproved by α-particle scattering.

The Geiger-Marsden experiment in which α-particles were fired at a thin gold foil; most passed through, some deflected, and a very few rebounded — showing the atom is mostly empty with a tiny dense nucleus.
An atomic model in which a tiny dense positively charged nucleus contains nearly all the mass, with electrons revolving around it in mostly empty space.
An atomic model in which electrons occupy definite circular orbits (energy levels) without radiating; they can jump between orbits by absorbing or emitting a single photon.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; uniquely identifies the element. Equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom.
Total number of nucleons (protons + neutrons) in the nucleus of an atom.
A region around the nucleus that can hold electrons of a particular energy. Labelled K, L, M, N, ... or n = 1, 2, 3, 4, ...
An electron in the outermost shell of an atom — determines the atom's chemical behaviour and valency.
The combining capacity of an element, deduced from valence electrons: equal to the count if ≤ 4, otherwise 8 − count. Noble gases have valency 0.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Atomic Structure (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-5 for Lesson 5. Attempt all questions. Refer to the periodic table for atomic numbers and atomic masses where needed.

questions.question: A figure shows α-particles being fired at a thin gold foil; most pass straight through, some deflect, and a few bounce back. (a) What does this figure show? (b) Who performed this experiment? (c) Explain in detail.
questions.answer:
(a) The figure shows the α-PARTICLE SCATTERING EXPERIMENT.
(b) Performed by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden in 1909, under the guidance of Ernest Rutherford.
(c) A stream of α-particles (helium nuclei, He²⁺) from a radioactive source was directed at a very thin sheet of gold foil. A fluorescent screen behind detected where the α-particles landed.
Three observations:
  1. MOST α-particles passed straight through the foil with no deflection — meaning most of the atom is empty space.
  2. A FEW were deflected through small angles — meaning they passed close to something positively charged that repelled them.
  3. A VERY FEW (about 1 in 8000) rebounded backward at large angles — meaning they had a head-on collision with something very dense and positive.
Rutherford interpreted these results to conclude that the atom has a tiny, dense, positively-charged NUCLEUS at the centre, surrounded by mostly empty space in which electrons revolve. This experiment overturned Thomson's plum-pudding model.
questions.explanation: Identify the experiment, the researchers, and the three observations and their interpretation.

questions.question: Write the electronic configuration of elements with 12, 14, 19, 23 and 26 protons.
questions.answer:
Apply the 2n² rule with the Bohr–Bury constraint (outermost shell ≤ 8 unless filling the d orbitals of a transition metal). For Z = 19 and beyond, the M shell can hold up to 18 but at this level we use the simple K(2), L(8), M(8 or up to 18), N filling.

 Z = 12 (Magnesium): 2, 8, 2.
 Z = 14 (Silicon):   2, 8, 4.
 Z = 19 (Potassium): 2, 8, 8, 1.
 Z = 23 (Vanadium):  2, 8, 11, 2 (transition metal; M shell continues to fill beyond 8).
 Z = 26 (Iron):      2, 8, 14, 2.

For the lower three (Mg, Si, K), the standard outer-shell-of-8 rule applies cleanly. For V and Fe, the M shell is filling its d sub-shells, which is why the M count is >8 — this is the start of the transition-metal series.
questions.explanation: Use 2n² + the outermost-≤-8 rule for the first 18 elements; for Z ≥ 19, allow the M shell to continue filling.

questions.question: Explain the plum-pudding model of the atom.
questions.answer:
Proposed by J. J. Thomson in 1903 (after his discovery of the electron in 1897). The atom is pictured as a uniform sphere of POSITIVE charge with the negatively-charged electrons scattered throughout — like plums embedded in a pudding (or seeds in a watermelon). The positive 'pudding' balances the total negative charge of the electrons, so the atom is electrically neutral.

Why it was eventually rejected: it could not explain the results of the α-particle scattering experiment (1909). If the positive charge were spread out as a 'pudding', no α-particle should bounce back at large angles — the observed large-angle rebounds proved that the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus, not spread out.
questions.explanation: Description + the experimental reason for its rejection.

questions.question: In what way are the different atomic particles arranged in the atom? Explain with reasons.
questions.answer:
The atom has TWO distinct regions:
  1. NUCLEUS at the centre — contains all the PROTONS (positively charged) and NEUTRONS (uncharged). The nucleus is extremely small (~10⁻¹⁵ m) but contains essentially all the atom's mass.
  2. EXTRANUCLEAR SPACE — the ELECTRONS revolve around the nucleus in shells (energy levels) labelled K, L, M, N, .... The atom is mostly this empty space (atomic diameter ~10⁻¹⁰ m, so the nucleus is about 100 000 times smaller than the whole atom).

Reasons for this arrangement:
  - Rutherford's α-scattering: showed all positive charge + mass is in a tiny central nucleus; most space is empty.
  - Bohr: showed electrons stay in stable orbits without radiating (postulate 1); jumps between orbits explain spectral lines (postulate 2).
  - The number of electrons equals the number of protons in a neutral atom; both equal the atomic number Z.
  - Shell capacity is 2n²; outermost ≤ 8 electrons (Bohr-Bury rule).
questions.explanation: Nucleus (p, n) + electrons in shells around it; justify with Rutherford and Bohr.

questions.question: Helium has 2 electrons in its outermost shell, but its valency is 0. Explain.
questions.answer:
Helium has electronic configuration 2 — its only shell (the K shell, n = 1) is COMPLETELY FILLED with the maximum 2 electrons allowed by 2n² (2·1² = 2).

An atom is chemically stable (unreactive) when its outermost shell is full. Helium's outer shell is full, so it has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons — no chemical bonds are formed. Hence valency = 0 (it cannot combine with other atoms).

The usual rule 'if valence electrons ≤ 4, valency = count' would have predicted valency 2 for helium, but the rule applies only when the outermost shell is INCOMPLETE. For helium (and all noble gases like Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe), the outermost shell is full and the noble-gas rule (valency = 0) takes precedence.
questions.explanation: Helium has a complete K shell — noble gas behaviour overrides the count-based valency rule.

questions.question: 'The number of protons and electrons in an atom and its corresponding ion are different.' Justify.
questions.answer:
In a neutral ATOM, the number of protons (Z) equals the number of electrons. So the atom carries no net charge.

An ION is an atom (or group of atoms) that has GAINED or LOST one or more electrons. The number of PROTONS is unchanged (it's still the same element), but the number of ELECTRONS differs from Z by the number of electrons lost or gained.
  - A CATION has FEWER electrons than protons → net positive charge. Example: Na (Z = 11; 11 e⁻) → Na⁺ (still 11 protons but only 10 e⁻).
  - An ANION has MORE electrons than protons → net negative charge. Example: Cl (Z = 17; 17 e⁻) → Cl⁻ (still 17 protons but 18 e⁻).

So the statement is true: in a neutral atom, protons = electrons; in an ion of the same element, protons ≠ electrons.
questions.explanation: Definitions of cation and anion; protons fixed, electrons change.

questions.question: If an atom has 6 electrons in its outermost shell, can it be considered a noble gas if it accepts 2 electrons? Comment.
questions.answer:
Let's see. An atom with 6 valence electrons accepts 2 more, ending up with 8 valence electrons — a complete octet, just like the noble gas argon (or neon, in the second-row case). Chemically, the atom now has a STABLE noble-gas-like electronic configuration.

BUT it is NOT a noble gas — because gaining 2 electrons makes it an ION, not a noble-gas atom. For example:
  Oxygen O (Z = 8; configuration 2, 6) + 2 e⁻ → O²⁻ (configuration 2, 8) — isoelectronic with neon.
The O²⁻ ion has a neon-like electron arrangement but is still oxygen (8 protons in its nucleus). It now carries a 2− charge. It can form ionic compounds like Na₂O or MgO. So while it achieves noble-gas STABILITY in its electrons, it is not chemically a noble gas (which would be uncharged and unreactive in monatomic form).
questions.explanation: Gaining electrons gives noble-gas electron configuration, but the atom becomes an ion — not a noble gas.

questions.question: 'Noble gases such as Argon, Neon, Xenon are unreactive.' Give the reason.
questions.answer:
Noble gases have COMPLETE OUTERMOST SHELLS:
  Helium: 2 (full K shell with 2 electrons).
  Neon: 2, 8 (full K and L shells; 8 outer-shell electrons).
  Argon: 2, 8, 8 (8 outer-shell electrons).
  Krypton, Xenon, Radon: also have 8 valence electrons.

A full outer shell is the most stable electronic configuration. Because of this, noble-gas atoms have NO TENDENCY to gain, lose or share electrons — so they don't form chemical bonds under ordinary conditions. They exist as monatomic gases. Their valency is 0 and their chemical reactivity is extremely low (a few compounds of xenon and krypton with very electronegative elements like F and O exist, but only under extreme conditions).

In fact, all other elements try to achieve a noble-gas electron configuration when they react — this is the basis of the OCTET RULE.
questions.explanation: Full outer shell → no driving force to bond. Hence chemically inert.

questions.question: Calculate the number of protons, electrons, neutrons in: Chlorine, Bromine, Iodine, Phosphorus, Silver and Gold. Also state their atomic number and mass number.
questions.answer:
Using p = electrons = Z, A = mass number, n = A − Z:

 Chlorine Cl: Z = 17, A = 35 (most common isotope). p = 17, e = 17, n = 35 − 17 = 18.
 Bromine Br: Z = 35, A = 80 (avg). p = 35, e = 35, n = 80 − 35 = 45.
 Iodine I:    Z = 53, A = 127. p = 53, e = 53, n = 127 − 53 = 74.
 Phosphorus P: Z = 15, A = 31. p = 15, e = 15, n = 31 − 15 = 16.
 Silver Ag:   Z = 47, A = 108 (avg). p = 47, e = 47, n = 108 − 47 = 61.
 Gold Au:     Z = 79, A = 197. p = 79, e = 79, n = 197 − 79 = 118.

(Where A is given as an average atomic mass, the neutron count is approximate; for the dominant isotope ²⁰⁷Au or ¹⁹⁷Au etc., n = A − Z exactly.)
questions.explanation: Apply p = Z, e = Z (neutral), n = A − Z. Use periodic table values.

questions.question: Is there an older idea of valency? If yes, what is the new concept of valency? Justify.
questions.answer:
Yes — historically valency was just an empirical concept: 'the combining capacity of an element' as observed from how many hydrogen (or chlorine) atoms it could combine with. There was no theoretical explanation — it was simply a number associated with each element.

The new (modern) concept relates valency to ELECTRONIC STRUCTURE:
  - Valence electrons = electrons in the outermost shell.
  - Atoms react to achieve a stable noble-gas electron configuration (full outer shell).
  - If valence electrons ≤ 4, the atom tends to LOSE them → valency = number of valence electrons.
  - If valence electrons > 4, the atom tends to GAIN electrons to fill its outer shell → valency = 8 − (valence electrons).
  - Noble gases (full shell) have valency 0.

Why this is better: it EXPLAINS why each element has the valency it does, predicts the type of bonds (ionic vs covalent) the element prefers, and integrates with the periodic table — elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and therefore the same valency.
questions.explanation: Old: empirical combining capacity. New: based on the electronic configuration of the outermost shell.

The valency of an element with electronic configuration 2, 8, 5 is ____.
The valency of any noble gas is ____.
For shell n = 3 (M shell), the formula 2n² gives a maximum of ____ electrons.
Name the two atomic constituent particles that (a) have equal and opposite charges, (b) have nearly equal masses, (c) are present in the nucleus.
questions.answer:
(a) Electron and proton — both carry the same magnitude of charge but opposite sign (electron −1, proton +1).
(b) Proton and neutron — both have mass close to 1 u (the electron is about 1836 times lighter).
(c) Proton and neutron — together they form the nucleus.

questions.question: How does an orbit differ from a shell?
questions.answer:
An ORBIT is a two-dimensional path (a circle, in Bohr's original model) that an electron follows around the nucleus — a specific, definite trajectory in a plane. A SHELL is a three-dimensional REGION around the nucleus in which an electron of a particular energy is likely to be found — it doesn't specify a definite path, only an energy and an average distance.
Bohr's original concept was an orbit; the modern quantum-mechanical concept is a shell (and within a shell, sub-shells and orbitals). Shells are still labelled K, L, M, N, ... but they describe energy levels and probability distributions, not fixed circular paths.

questions.question: Which atomic model could not explain the results of the α-particle scattering experiment?
questions.answer: Thomson's PLUM-PUDDING model. It pictured the atom as a uniform sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded — but this could not explain why some α-particles bounced back from a thin foil. A uniform positive 'pudding' would deflect α-particles only weakly. The large-angle scattering observed implied a concentrated dense positive nucleus — which is what Rutherford then proposed.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of electrons that can be present in the N shell?
questions.answer: For the N shell, n = 4. The maximum is 2n² = 2 × 4² = 32 electrons. (However, as the OUTERMOST shell, it cannot hold more than 8 electrons at the time of filling. The 18-, 32-electron capacities only show up after the next shell starts filling — when N is no longer the outermost shell.)

questions.question: Find the number of electrons, protons and neutrons in the atom ¹⁷₈X.
questions.answer:
From the notation ¹⁷₈X: Z = 8 (subscript) so PROTONS = 8 and ELECTRONS = 8 (neutral atom). A = 17 (superscript), so NEUTRONS = A − Z = 17 − 8 = 9.
This is the isotope oxygen-17 (¹⁷O), one of the three naturally-occurring oxygen isotopes.

questions.question: State three observations that contradicted Dalton's atomic theory.
questions.answer:
(1) DIVISIBILITY OF ATOMS — Dalton said atoms are indivisible; but the discoveries of the electron (Thomson 1897), the proton (Goldstein/Rutherford) and the neutron (Chadwick 1932) showed atoms have internal structure.
(2) ATOMS OF SAME ELEMENT NOT ALWAYS IDENTICAL — Dalton said all atoms of an element are identical; but ISOTOPES (e.g. ¹⁶O, ¹⁷O, ¹⁸O) have the same Z but different masses.
(3) ATOMS OF DIFFERENT ELEMENTS CAN HAVE EQUAL MASS — Dalton said different elements have different atomic masses; but ISOBARS (e.g. ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca) have the same mass number with different Z.

questions.question: State three drawbacks of Rutherford's atomic model.
questions.answer:
(1) STABILITY PROBLEM — by Maxwell's electromagnetic theory, an accelerating charged particle continuously radiates energy. An electron orbiting the nucleus is accelerating (its direction changes), so it should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus within ~10⁻⁸ s. But atoms are stable — so the model is incomplete.
(2) NO ELECTRON ARRANGEMENT — Rutherford's model says nothing about HOW the electrons are arranged in space; it just says they're 'around the nucleus'.
(3) NO EXPLANATION OF SPECTRA — atoms emit only certain discrete frequencies of light when excited (line spectra). Rutherford's model gives no reason for this discreteness. (Bohr's later model fixed all three problems.)

questions.question: State Bohr's two postulates.
questions.answer:
Postulate 1: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in CERTAIN PERMITTED CIRCULAR ORBITS (shells / energy levels) labelled K, L, M, N, .... While in these orbits, the electron does NOT emit or absorb energy. The K shell has the lowest energy.

Postulate 2: Electrons can JUMP between shells by absorbing or emitting a photon of energy equal to the difference between the two levels: hν = E_f − E_i (absorbed when going up, emitted when going down).

questions.question: Write the electronic configurations of Mg (Z = 12), Si (Z = 14) and K (Z = 19).
questions.answer:
Mg (Z = 12): 2, 8, 2 (K = 2, L = 8, M = 2).
Si (Z = 14): 2, 8, 4 (K = 2, L = 8, M = 4).
K (Z = 19): 2, 8, 8, 1 (K = 2, L = 8, M = 8, N = 1). The 19th electron goes into the N shell rather than completing the M shell — because the M shell, when it's the outermost shell, can only hold 8 electrons (Bohr-Bury rule).

questions.question: An element has valency 4 and electrons in the K, L and M shells. Find Z.
questions.answer: Valency 4 with valence electrons ≤ 4 means there are 4 valence electrons in the outermost shell. The outermost shell is M (the question says K, L and M shells are occupied). K = 2 (full), L = 8 (full), M = 4. Total electrons = 2 + 8 + 4 = 14. For a neutral atom, electrons = protons = Z = 14. The element is silicon (Si).

questions.question: Which observation about ordinary matter helped to reject one of the early atomic models?
questions.answer: The OBSERVED STABILITY of matter (atoms don't collapse — the world around us is built of stable atoms) was the observation that rejected RUTHERFORD'S model. According to Rutherford's model, electrons orbiting the nucleus should radiate energy continuously and spiral into the nucleus, causing the atom to collapse within nanoseconds. Since this does not happen, Rutherford's model was incomplete. Bohr fixed this by proposing that electrons in allowed orbits do not radiate.

questions.question: For each, write the valency: (i) Li (Z = 3), (ii) F (Z = 9), (iii) Mg (Z = 12), (iv) Cl (Z = 17), (v) Ne (Z = 10).
questions.answer:
(i) Li (config 2, 1) — 1 valence electron → valency 1.
(ii) F (config 2, 7) — 7 valence electrons → valency 8 − 7 = 1.
(iii) Mg (config 2, 8, 2) — 2 valence electrons → valency 2.
(iv) Cl (config 2, 8, 7) — 7 valence electrons → valency 8 − 7 = 1.
(v) Ne (config 2, 8) — full outer shell → valency 0 (noble gas).

questions.question: Why did most α-particles in the Geiger-Marsden experiment pass straight through the gold foil?
questions.answer: Because the ATOM IS MOSTLY EMPTY SPACE. The positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus (~10⁻¹⁵ m across) in the centre of a much larger atom (~10⁻¹⁰ m across). Most α-particles pass through gaps in the atomic structure without encountering the nucleus, and so are not deflected at all.

questions.question: How is an atom electrically neutral?
questions.answer: In a neutral atom, the number of POSITIVE charges (protons in the nucleus, each +1) equals the number of NEGATIVE charges (electrons around the nucleus, each −1). The total charge is therefore zero. If an atom gains or loses electrons, this balance is disturbed and it becomes an ion (cation or anion).

questions.question: Why does sodium have valency 1 and chlorine have valency 1, but they form NaCl rather than NaCl₂?
questions.answer:
Sodium (Z = 11; configuration 2, 8, 1) has 1 valence electron — it tends to LOSE that one electron and become Na⁺ (configuration 2, 8 — like neon). Valency 1 means it forms one bond.

Chlorine (Z = 17; configuration 2, 8, 7) has 7 valence electrons — it tends to GAIN one electron to become Cl⁻ (configuration 2, 8, 8 — like argon). Valency 1 means it accepts one bond.

When Na meets Cl, one electron transfers: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ and Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻. The +1 cation and −1 anion attract each other to form NaCl (1:1 ratio). NaCl₂ would require 2 Cl⁻ per Na⁺, which would mean Na had given up 2 electrons — but Na only has 1 valence electron to give. So 1:1 ratio is the only possibility, giving the formula NaCl.

questions.question: How many electrons are in the second shell (L shell) of (a) carbon Z=6, (b) chlorine Z=17?
questions.answer:
(a) Carbon (Z=6): configuration 2, 4 — L shell has 4 electrons.
(b) Chlorine (Z=17): configuration 2, 8, 7 — L shell has 8 electrons (it is completely filled; the remaining 7 are in M).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In 1897 J. J. Thomson passed a high voltage between electrodes in a glass tube containing gas at very low pressure. He observed rays travelling from the cathode toward the anode that were deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

(i) What did Thomson call these rays?
(ii) What did he discover about the particles?
(iii) What is the relative charge and mass of the discovered particle?
(iv) Why was this discovery important for atomic theory?
questions.answer:
(i) CATHODE RAYS.
(ii) The rays consisted of negatively charged particles that exist in all atoms — Thomson named them ELECTRONS.
(iii) Charge = −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (relative charge −1). Mass ≈ 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg — about 1/1836 of a proton's mass.
(iv) It showed that ATOMS ARE NOT INDIVISIBLE, contrary to Dalton's theory. Atoms must contain internal subatomic particles. This was the first step toward modern atomic structure.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In the Geiger-Marsden α-scattering experiment, α-particles were fired at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through; a few deflected by small angles; very few bounced back at large angles.

(i) What did Rutherford conclude from observation (1)?
(ii) What did he conclude from observation (3)?
(iii) Sketch (in words) Rutherford's nuclear model.
(iv) Name one drawback of Rutherford's model.
questions.answer:
(i) Most α-particles pass through ⇒ the atom is MOSTLY EMPTY SPACE.
(ii) A few rebound backward ⇒ there is a tiny, dense, positively-charged region within the atom — the NUCLEUS — that repels the positive α-particles when hit head-on.
(iii) The atom has a tiny dense nucleus at the centre containing all the protons (positive charge) and essentially all the mass. The electrons revolve around the nucleus at much greater distances, in mostly empty space. The atom is electrically neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
(iv) Drawback: a circling electron should continuously radiate (Maxwell) and spiral into the nucleus, but atoms are stable. (Also: model doesn't specify HOW electrons are arranged or explain atomic spectra.)

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Niels Bohr (1913) proposed that electrons in an atom occupy DEFINITE circular orbits and do not radiate while in those orbits. They can jump between orbits by absorbing or emitting a single photon.

(i) State Bohr's two postulates.
(ii) How does postulate 1 explain the stability of atoms?
(iii) How does postulate 2 explain the appearance of DISCRETE spectral lines emitted by excited atoms?
(iv) What is the symbol for the shell of lowest energy?
questions.answer:
(i) Postulate 1: Electrons orbit only in certain discrete shells (K, L, M, N, ...). While in these orbits they do NOT radiate energy. Postulate 2: An electron can move between shells by absorbing (going up) or emitting (going down) a single photon of energy hν = |E_f − E_i|.
(ii) Since electrons in allowed orbits don't radiate, they don't spiral into the nucleus. The atom is therefore stable — fixing Rutherford's model.
(iii) Because the shells have DISCRETE energies, only specific transitions are allowed, and each transition emits a photon of a SPECIFIC energy (and hence frequency / wavelength). This is why atomic spectra consist of discrete LINES rather than a continuous distribution.
(iv) K (n = 1).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by 2n². However, the OUTERMOST shell cannot hold more than 8 electrons (the Bohr-Bury rule).

(i) What is the maximum capacity of each of the K, L, M and N shells?
(ii) Write the electronic configuration of Ar (Z=18).
(iii) Write the electronic configuration of K (Z=19).
(iv) Why doesn't the 19th electron go into the M shell?
questions.answer:
(i) K (n=1): 2; L (n=2): 8; M (n=3): 18; N (n=4): 32.
(ii) Ar: 2, 8, 8. Outermost (M) is fully complete with 8 — Ar is a noble gas.
(iii) K: 2, 8, 8, 1. The 19th electron goes into the N shell.
(iv) Because once Ar has 8 in the M shell (as its outermost shell), the next electron added must go to the NEXT shell up — the outermost shell can never exceed 8 at the time the next electron is filled. So the 19th electron starts the N shell. (Only after some N-shell electrons are present does the M shell begin to fill beyond 8, with d-orbital filling for transition metals.)

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The combining capacity (valency) of an element is determined by its valence electrons (the electrons in the outermost shell). If the count is ≤ 4, the valency equals the count; if > 4, the valency is 8 minus the count. Noble gases (full outer shell) have valency 0.

(i) Find the valency of Mg (config 2, 8, 2).
(ii) Find the valency of S (config 2, 8, 6).
(iii) Find the valency of Cl (config 2, 8, 7).
(iv) Find the valency of Ne (config 2, 8).
questions.answer:
(i) Mg: 2 valence electrons (≤ 4) → valency 2.
(ii) S: 6 valence electrons (> 4) → valency 8 − 6 = 2.
(iii) Cl: 7 valence electrons (> 4) → valency 8 − 7 = 1.
(iv) Ne: 8 valence electrons — full outer shell → valency 0 (noble gas).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Ions are formed when an atom gains or loses electrons. A cation is a positive ion (lost electrons); an anion is a negative ion (gained electrons). The number of protons is unchanged.

(i) Na (Z = 11) loses 1 electron to form Na⁺. How many protons and electrons does Na⁺ have?
(ii) Cl (Z = 17) gains 1 electron to form Cl⁻. How many protons and electrons does Cl⁻ have?
(iii) Write the electronic configuration of Na⁺ and Cl⁻.
(iv) Which noble gas has the same electron configuration as Na⁺? As Cl⁻?
questions.answer:
(i) Na⁺: protons = 11 (unchanged); electrons = 11 − 1 = 10.
(ii) Cl⁻: protons = 17 (unchanged); electrons = 17 + 1 = 18.
(iii) Na⁺ config: 2, 8 (10 electrons). Cl⁻ config: 2, 8, 8 (18 electrons).
(iv) Na⁺ is isoelectronic with NEON (Z = 10, config 2, 8). Cl⁻ is isoelectronic with ARGON (Z = 18, config 2, 8, 8). Achieving a noble-gas electron configuration is what drives atoms to form these ions.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A particular atom has 20 protons, 20 neutrons and 20 electrons.

(i) What is its atomic number Z?
(ii) What is its mass number A?
(iii) Identify the element.
(iv) Write its electronic configuration and predict its valency.
questions.answer:
(i) Z = 20 (number of protons).
(ii) A = 20 + 20 = 40 (protons + neutrons).
(iii) Z = 20 is CALCIUM (Ca), and A = 40 is its most abundant natural isotope.
(iv) Configuration: K = 2, L = 8, M = 8, N = 2 → 2, 8, 8, 2. 2 valence electrons (≤ 4) → valency = 2. Calcium loses both valence electrons to form Ca²⁺ (achieving Ar-like configuration), and forms compounds like CaO, CaCl₂, CaCO₃.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student claims: 'Thomson's plum-pudding model wasn't completely wrong — it did correctly predict that atoms contain electrons.'

(i) Is the student's statement valid? Justify.
(ii) What part of the plum-pudding model was correct?
(iii) What was the fatal flaw of the model?
(iv) Who fixed the flaw and how?
questions.answer:
(i) Yes — the student is partly right. Thomson's model was the FIRST attempt to incorporate the electron (which Thomson himself had discovered) into the structure of the atom. It correctly recognised that atoms contain electrons.
(ii) The correct insight: ATOMS CONTAIN ELECTRONS, and atoms are electrically NEUTRAL overall (the positive 'pudding' balanced the electrons). It also correctly placed the electrons within the atom.
(iii) Flaw: the positive charge was pictured as SPREAD OUT uniformly across the entire atomic volume. This made the model unable to explain α-particle scattering — particles should never bounce back from a diffuse positive pudding.
(iv) Rutherford (1911) fixed it by concluding from the α-scattering observations that the positive charge (and most of the mass) is concentrated in a tiny dense NUCLEUS at the centre — replacing the spread-out 'pudding' with a point-like centre.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Rutherford's nuclear model was a major advance, but it had three serious drawbacks.

(i) What does Maxwell's electromagnetic theory predict about an orbiting electron?
(ii) Why does this make Rutherford's atom unstable?
(iii) Why is the observed stability of matter contradictory to this?
(iv) How did Bohr resolve this stability problem?
questions.answer:
(i) Maxwell's theory says any ACCELERATING charged particle continuously radiates electromagnetic energy. An electron in a circular orbit is constantly being accelerated (its direction changes even if its speed is constant).
(ii) If electrons radiate energy continuously, they lose kinetic energy and spiral inward toward the nucleus. Theoretical estimates put the time-to-collapse at about 10⁻⁸ seconds.
(iii) Observed matter — every atom around us — has been stable for billions of years. If Rutherford's prediction were correct, no stable atom could exist for more than a microscopic instant. So the observation of stable matter directly contradicts the prediction.
(iv) Bohr (1913) postulated that electrons occupy DEFINITE quantised orbits (shells), and that while in these orbits they do NOT radiate energy. Radiation only happens when an electron transitions between shells. This kept atoms stable while explaining the discrete spectral lines, which neither classical physics nor Rutherford's model could.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Write the electronic configurations of all the elements from Z = 1 to Z = 10. (Hydrogen to Neon.)

(i) List them in tabular form: element name, symbol, Z, configuration.
(ii) Group these by 'noble gas (full outer shell)' and 'others'.
(iii) Which two elements have similar chemical behaviour and why?
(iv) State the valency of each.
questions.answer:
(i)
 H Hydrogen   Z=1  → 1
 He Helium     Z=2  → 2
 Li Lithium    Z=3  → 2, 1
 Be Beryllium  Z=4  → 2, 2
 B Boron       Z=5  → 2, 3
 C Carbon      Z=6  → 2, 4
 N Nitrogen    Z=7  → 2, 5
 O Oxygen      Z=8  → 2, 6
 F Fluorine    Z=9  → 2, 7
 Ne Neon       Z=10 → 2, 8

(ii) Noble gases (full outer shell): He (2 — K full); Ne (2, 8 — L full). Others: H, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F.
(iii) Hydrogen (1 valence e⁻) and lithium (1 valence e⁻) — both have 1 outer electron, both have valency 1, and both readily form +1 cations (H⁺, Li⁺). They differ in shell number but are chemically related.
(iv) Valencies: H = 1; He = 0; Li = 1; Be = 2; B = 3; C = 4; N = 3 (8 − 5); O = 2 (8 − 6); F = 1 (8 − 7); Ne = 0.

questions.question: State two postulates of Dalton's atomic theory.
questions.answer:
(1) All matter is composed of indivisible particles called ATOMS.
(2) Atoms of the same element are identical (same mass and properties). Atoms of different elements differ. (Additional postulates: atoms combine in small whole-number ratios; atoms are conserved in chemical reactions.)

questions.question: Briefly describe the experiment by which J. J. Thomson discovered the electron.
questions.answer: Thomson used a CATHODE RAY TUBE — a sealed glass tube containing gas at very low pressure with two electrodes connected to a high voltage. When voltage was applied, glowing 'rays' (cathode rays) travelled from the cathode (−) to the anode (+). Thomson showed these rays were deflected by both electric and magnetic fields in directions consistent with negative charge, with the same charge-to-mass ratio regardless of the gas used. He concluded that they were negatively charged particles common to all atoms — and named them ELECTRONS.

questions.question: Tabulate the mass, charge and relative charge of the electron, proton and neutron.
questions.answer:
Particle  Mass (kg)              Charge (C)              Relative charge
  Electron  9.11 × 10⁻³¹           −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹            −1
  Proton    1.67 × 10⁻²⁷           +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹            +1
  Neutron   1.675 × 10⁻²⁷          0                       0

questions.question: Describe the plum-pudding model. Who proposed it and what was its main shortcoming?
questions.answer:
Thomson (1903) proposed the plum-pudding model: an atom is a uniform sphere of POSITIVE charge with electrons embedded throughout — like plums in a pudding. The positive 'pudding' balances the negative electrons, making the atom neutral.
Main shortcoming: cannot explain the LARGE-ANGLE DEFLECTIONS of α-particles in Rutherford's gold-foil experiment. A diffuse positive pudding cannot turn a fast-moving α-particle through a large angle, let alone rebound it. The experiment proved that the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny dense nucleus, not spread out as a 'pudding'.

questions.question: Describe in three or four sentences Rutherford's α-particle scattering experiment and the conclusion he drew.
questions.answer: Geiger and Marsden (under Rutherford, 1909) fired a beam of α-particles at a very thin gold foil and observed them with a fluorescent screen. Most α-particles passed straight through the foil (showing the atom is mostly empty space); a few were deflected by small angles; a very small fraction (about 1 in 8000) rebounded back at large angles (showing they hit something very dense and positive head-on). Rutherford concluded that all of the atom's positive charge and essentially all of its mass is concentrated in a tiny dense NUCLEUS at the centre, with electrons revolving around it in mostly empty space.

questions.question: State the two postulates of Bohr's model.
questions.answer:
Postulate 1: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in CERTAIN PERMITTED CIRCULAR ORBITS / SHELLS (labelled K, L, M, N, ...). While in an allowed orbit, the electron does NOT radiate energy.
Postulate 2: An electron can JUMP between shells by absorbing or emitting a single PHOTON whose energy equals the difference between the two shells' energies (E_photon = hν = |E_f − E_i|).

questions.question: Write the electronic configurations of: (i) carbon (Z=6), (ii) sodium (Z=11), (iii) chlorine (Z=17), (iv) calcium (Z=20).
questions.answer:
(i) Carbon: 2, 4.
(ii) Sodium: 2, 8, 1.
(iii) Chlorine: 2, 8, 7.
(iv) Calcium: 2, 8, 8, 2.

questions.question: Determine the valency of each: (i) Be (Z=4), (ii) N (Z=7), (iii) Cl (Z=17), (iv) Ar (Z=18).
questions.answer:
(i) Be (2, 2): 2 valence electrons → valency 2.
(ii) N (2, 5): 5 valence electrons → 8 − 5 = 3.
(iii) Cl (2, 8, 7): 7 valence electrons → 8 − 7 = 1.
(iv) Ar (2, 8, 8): full outer shell → valency 0 (noble gas).

questions.question: Why do all noble gases have valency 0? Use sodium as a counter-example.
questions.answer:
Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) have FULL outermost shells (He: 2 in K; the others: 8 in their outer shell). A full outer shell is the most stable electronic configuration — there's no driving force for the atom to gain, lose or share electrons. So they form no bonds → valency 0.

Counter-example: sodium has configuration 2, 8, 1. Its outer shell is INCOMPLETE (only 1 electron). Losing that one electron leaves it with a noble-gas configuration (2, 8 — like Ne) and a +1 charge. This is favourable, so sodium readily reacts. Valency is 1.

questions.question: How does the experiment with anode rays show that protons exist in atoms?
List the three drawbacks of Rutherford's nuclear model.
questions.answer:
(1) ATOMIC STABILITY PROBLEM: Maxwell's electromagnetic theory predicts that an accelerating charged particle continuously radiates energy. An orbiting electron is accelerating (direction changes), so it should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus within nanoseconds. Real atoms are stable for billions of years.
(2) NO ELECTRON ARRANGEMENT: the model says electrons revolve 'around' the nucleus but doesn't specify HOW they're arranged — in which orbits, at what distances, with what energies.
(3) NO EXPLANATION OF SPECTRA: atoms emit only specific DISCRETE frequencies of light when excited (line spectra). Rutherford's model offers no reason for this discreteness; it would predict continuous emission.

questions.question: How does Bohr's model resolve Rutherford's stability problem?
questions.answer: By introducing QUANTISATION. Bohr's first postulate states that electrons can occupy ONLY certain permitted orbits (shells), and that while in any one of these allowed orbits the electron does NOT radiate energy. This violates classical electromagnetic theory but is consistent with the observation that atoms are stable. Electrons therefore remain in their orbits indefinitely without spiralling into the nucleus. Energy is emitted or absorbed only during transitions between orbits — explaining both atomic stability and the discrete line spectra of excited atoms.

questions.question: Show that for Z = 19 (potassium), the 19th electron must go into the N shell, not the M shell.
questions.answer:
Filling sequentially:
 - K shell holds max 2. Electrons 1 and 2 fill it. (After 2 e⁻: configuration 2.)
 - L shell holds max 8. Electrons 3-10 fill it. (After 10 e⁻: configuration 2, 8.)
 - M shell could in principle hold 18 (2 × 3² = 18). Electrons 11-18 fill 8 of them. (After 18 e⁻: configuration 2, 8, 8 — argon.)
 - Now the M shell has 8 electrons and is the OUTERMOST shell. The Bohr-Bury rule says the outermost shell cannot hold more than 8 electrons (during filling). So the 19th electron cannot go into M.
 - It must go into the next shell: N. After 19 e⁻: configuration 2, 8, 8, 1 — this is potassium. (Later, with even higher Z, the M shell can fill beyond 8 once it's no longer outermost — that's where transition metals come from.)

questions.question: Two atoms have valence-electron counts 1 and 7. What kind of bond would they form?
questions.answer:
An atom with 1 valence electron (e.g. Na) wants to LOSE its valence electron to achieve a noble-gas configuration.
An atom with 7 valence electrons (e.g. Cl) wants to GAIN one electron to complete its outer shell.

When these atoms meet, the electron transfers from the metal to the non-metal: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻. The resulting +1 cation and −1 anion attract each other electrostatically — an IONIC BOND. Example: NaCl (table salt). The 1:1 ratio is fixed because each Na donates exactly 1 electron and each Cl accepts exactly 1.

So: 1 valence + 7 valence → ionic compound, formula M⁺X⁻ (1:1).
